newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Nomura sprang from money changer roots.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Nomura sprang from money changer roots.

text.p: Nomura Securities Co Ltd, now at the heart of a racketeer payoff scandal, has been a key part of Japan's financial system since the days of its 19th century founding by a money changer.

The present firm, which employs nearly 11,000 staff in dozens of offices around the world and dominates both share and bond trading in Japan, sprang from an Osaka money-changing shop set up in 1872 by Tokushichi Nomura, the illegitimate son of a samurai warrior.
His son, Tokushichi Nomura II, enlarged the business and incorporated it in 1925 as Osaka Nomura Bank.
The son, who died in 1945, was an acknowledged financial wizard whose gains in share dealings earned him the name, "The Great General of the Stock Market".
Nomura Securities grew out of the breakup of the bank.
It started by trading bonds, expanding into securities in 1938, and in 1941 became the first Japanese firm to start investment trust operations.

Most of the Nomura fortune was lost in the ruins of World War Two. But the firm, no longer family-owned, quickly recovered and achieved global prominence by underwriting companies such as Sony Corp that were at the heart of Japan's postwar economic miracle.
In 1969, as a key component of a relentless overseas expansion, the firm set up Nomura Securities International in the United States. In 1972, it set up Nomura Europe.
It exerts a powerful influence on every aspect of business in the yen bond market and is also Japan's top foreign bond seller.
The latest scandal is the second to hit the company in less than a decade.

In a previous scandal in 1991, Nomura and other leading Japanese brokerages were found to have paid improper compensation to favoured clients. Top executives at Nomura resigned in 1991 in response to the affair and revelations that affiliates had done deals with gangsters.
